idiom_name: JsonConverter<T> with Read/Write, applied via [JsonConverter] or JsonSerializerOptions.Converters
implementation_notes: The modern default: derive from JsonConverter<T> and override Read(ref Utf8JsonReader, Type, JsonSerializerOptions) and Write(Utf8JsonWriter, T, JsonSerializerOptions); one class owns both directions and is attached with [JsonConverter(typeof(...))] or registered in the options, so neither the DTO nor the serialization layer references the other. JsonConverterFactory is needed only for open generics or enums; the hand-written mapper class survives when the second representation is not JSON.
pitfalls: Read receives the reader positioned on the current token and cannot read ahead, so a converter that assumes the whole payload is buffered fails on larger documents.
A converter registered in JsonSerializerOptions rewrites every matching member in the graph (including dictionary keys); the narrow [JsonConverter] attribute is usually safer.
Silently returning default(T) turns a malformed payload into a valid-looking empty object - failing conversions should throw so the caller sees a JsonException.

variants.name: EF Core ValueConverter<TModel,TProvider> for persistence
variants.implementation_notes: Persistence-facing realization: a ValueConverter<TModel,TProvider> (or the two expression arguments to HasConversion) owns the column-to-model pair, is declared in OnModelCreating or ConfigureConventions, and leaves the entity and the database provider unaware of each other. The classic mapping class is replaced by the converter instance, and the model configuration is the only place that knows both sides.
pitfalls: Without a ValueComparer<T> change tracking compares mapped values by reference, so in-place mutations after a query are never detected or saved.
The converter never sees null: a NULL column is a null reference in the entity, so null-as-empty semantics must be handled outside the converter.
Queries translate through the conversion, so LINQ predicates over the converted property only work if the conversion is expressible in SQL.

variants.name: System.ComponentModel.TypeConverter (design-time classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The legacy, framework-wide realization: derive from TypeConverter, override CanConvertFrom/ConvertFrom and CanConvertTo/ConvertTo, attach it with [TypeConverter(typeof(...))], and TypeDescriptor.GetConverter(type) resolves it, so designers, property grids and configuration binders convert without knowing either type. It remains the right choice when the converting party is a designer or generic property editor rather than serialization code.
pitfalls: TypeDescriptor caches converters and their convertibility answers; a converter whose CanConvertFrom depends on mutable state replies stale results.
ConvertTo/ConvertFrom are culture- and context-sensitive by contract, so ignoring the CultureInfo argument yields values that parse differently per locale.
It is an ambient reflection-discovered mechanism: hard to see at the call site, and two converters claiming the same type interact silently.
